prompt: Write a short story about a first day at a new job. About 800 words. Output only the story, with no title.
raw:
The lost-and-found office of the Metropolitan Transit Authority was in a basement beneath the Fourth Street station, and on his first morning Theo walked past the door twice before he noticed it. It was painted the same gray as the wall. A small brass plate said only RECOVERY.

Inside, a woman in a cardigan the color of weak tea was eating a hard-boiled egg over a sheet of newspaper.

"You're the new one," she said. "I'm Doreen. Don't touch the umbrellas."

Theo looked to his left. There were umbrellas. There were, he would later estimate, nine hundred umbrellas, hung by their handles on long steel rods that ran the length of the room like a dry cleaner's conveyor. Black ones mostly, but also floral, plaid, one shaped like a duck's head.

"Why not?"

"Because you'll want to organize them, and you can't. Nobody can. I've been here twenty-two years and I've made peace with the umbrellas." She folded the eggshell into the newspaper with surgical care. "Coffee's in the back. Then I'll show you the intake."

Theo had taken the job because it was the first one that called him back. He'd spent eight months after graduation sending résumés into what felt like a well with no bottom, and when the city's HR office phoned, he said yes before they finished describing the position. Clerk II, Property Recovery. He'd imagined a counter, a ledger, maybe a lot of phones. He had not imagined the shelves.

They went back farther than the light did. Rows of gray metal shelving stacked with plastic bins, each bin labeled in Doreen's square handwriting: GLOVES (L), GLOVES (R), GLOVES (PAIRS, MIRACULOUS). KEYS — CAR. KEYS — HOUSE. KEYS — UNKNOWN PURPOSE. There was a bin for dentures. There was a bin for wedding rings that held, Theo saw when he peeked, at least thirty.

"People take them off," Doreen said, reading his face. "Before they get on the train. After. Who knows. Fights, mostly, I think."

"Does anyone come back for them?"

"Some." She pulled down a bin marked PROSTHETICS and showed him a single, elegant wooden leg. "This one's been here since 2009. I keep hoping."

Intake, it turned out, was the heart of the work. Every morning a man named Ruben arrived from the depot with a canvas cart full of what the city had left behind the day before. Theo's job was to log each item, tag it, and find it a home on the shelves. Doreen sat beside him for the first hour, correcting his descriptions.

"Not 'blue scarf,'" she said. "Nobody comes in looking for a blue scarf. They come in looking for *their* scarf. 'Navy wool, frayed at one end, smells like cloves.' That's somebody's scarf."

So Theo learned to look closer. A child's sneaker, left foot, light-up heel, one light broken. A paperback of *Middlemarch* with a grocery list as a bookmark: eggs, stamps, call Mom back. A violin case, empty, which bothered him more than he could explain. A Tupperware of homemade dumplings, still faintly warm, which Doreen declared perishable and, after a moment's solemn consideration, lunch.

Around two o'clock the bell above the door rang and a man in a postal uniform came in, out of breath.

"Glasses," he said. "Tortoiseshell. I left them on the 6 train, I think yesterday, maybe the day before. I can't read my route sheets."

Theo felt Doreen watching him. He went to the back, found EYEWEAR, and opened the bin. Forty pairs, at least. Half were tortoiseshell. He stood there, panic rising, and then remembered: *somebody's glasses*. He went back out.

"Can you tell me anything else about them?"

The man thought. "Left arm's a little bent. I sat on them once. And there's a scratch on the right lens, bottom corner. Like a little comet."

Theo went back. It took him six minutes, holding each pair up to the bare bulb, but he found the comet. When he handed them over, the man put them on, blinked, and laughed out loud, a short surprised bark, as if the world had just been handed back to him in focus.

"Thank you," he said. "Really. You don't know."

After he left, Doreen went back to her crossword without comment. But a few minutes later she slid a key across the desk toward him. It was small and brass and tagged with a strip of masking tape that read THEO.

"What's this for?"

"Your locker. Back by the umbrellas." She didn't look up. "Most people quit by lunch. They see the shelves and they think, this is just a warehouse of sad things."

"Isn't it?"

Doreen filled in a word, considered it, erased it.

"It's a waiting room," she said. "Everything here is waiting for someone to remember it."

At five o'clock Theo climbed the stairs into the evening rush, the platform loud and bright and crowded with people holding tight to their bags, their phones, their children's hands. He found himself watching them, cataloguing, wondering who would be coming to see him tomorrow.

He checked his pocket for the brass key. It was still there.
